idiom_name: rubocop-ast NodePattern DSL (def_node_matcher, def_node_search) over parser-gem or Prism nodes
implementation_notes: rubocop-ast turns the pattern into a string that compiles to Ruby: (send nil? :puts $_) matches a send node with no receiver named puts, using _ for any single node, ... for any number, *, + and ? for repetition, {a b} for a union, [] for and, $ for capture, ^ for a parent check and a backtick for descendants. def_node_matcher compiles a pattern into a method and def_node_search into a walking search, so the engine owns the walk and the method body is the action; trees come from the parser gem or Prism, and rewriting goes through rubocop-ast's TreeRewriter or Prism's node API. Prism nodes also implement deconstruct and deconstruct_keys, so a plain case/in can match them natively, while RubyVM::AbstractSyntaxTree nodes expose only type and children and are documented as implementation-specific - which is why the DSL, not the language, is the primary realization.
pitfalls: Patterns are strings compiled at definition time: a typo raises when the pattern is compiled or never matches at all, so use def_node_matcher (which validates on load) and unit-test each matcher with a positive node and a near miss.
The AST is a plain s-expression of symbols and nodes, so a pattern that omits the receiver position also matches self-calls; use nil? plus explicit child positions to pin the shape.
RuboCop re-runs an autocorrect on the corrected tree until it converges, so a rule that rewrites to a shape it still matches loops until the correction guard aborts the run.
